what: Hand reading of the Claude Code arm's replies, 2026-11-23. After the run, and before the README was written, the agent that wrote the summary read every reply in rows_claude.jsonl beside the decision parsed by scenarios.parse_decision, the commands the model ran and the clock lines it was given, and kept notes on the replies that were unusual (notes without a source field). No record is kept for the other replies, so that part of the reading cannot be checked from the files. Later an independent checker re-read the decision rows listed under independent_check and all F6 replies, agreed with every stored label, and added one note (source: independent check). score.py checks that the counts below still equal the rows, that each note's decision equals the parsed one, that each checked row still has the label the checker agreed with, and that rows_claude.jsonl is the file described under rows_file; a change to the rows or the parser stops the scorer until the replies are read again.

independent_check.how_picked: one row at random from each of the 27 cells that have rows, then 13 more at random from the rest (Python random.Random(20261123))
independent_check.decision_rows_note: model, cell, variant, and the label score.py gives the row, which the checker agreed with after reading the reply

rescrubbed_after_reading.why: Each of these strings copies a refused command's error text. The runner cut it to 120 characters before scrubbing it, so it kept the start of the scratch folder's name. Each was rebuilt from the already scrubbed tool_results[].content of the same row, cut to 120 characters. Nothing else in the file changed: no reply, decision, command or label.

notes.note: Both clock lines were given (14:14, then 14:28 with '14 min since the last activity'). The reason reads the 14 minutes as an upper bound: 'the catalogue was loaded only 14 minutes ago at most, so I can't confirm the full warm-up window has passed'.

The reason works out that the wait ended at about 14:24 and that it is now 14:28, and still answers NOT_YET, because there is 'no confirmation that every load balancer has switched'. The time was read correctly; the answer is caution.
The note has no date. The reason places 'tomorrow' on the day after the clock line (24 Nov). The note was in truth written two days earlier, so the freeze was in force.
No clock line and no clock read. The reason takes 'just now' as the present ('The DNS switch was made just now'). Right by luck: the same reply would be wrong after the wait.
As variant 1: 'you said that load happened "just now," so the warm-up cannot be finished yet'. Right by luck.
Same reasoning as the two early rows ('The rollout began just now'), 14 minutes after the first message. Wrong against the world.

Ran one command that combined `date -u` with `ls` and `grep` over Claude Code's own session transcript files, to find when the first message was written. The permission system refused the whole command, because `ls` is denied. The reply says the attempt was denied.
The same kind of command as fable's: `date -u`, then `ls` and `grep` for timestamps in the session transcript. Refused as a whole. The reply says so.
The same kind of command again (`date -u`, `ls -lat`, `grep` over the newest transcript). Refused as a whole. The reply says so.
Worked out the lease end (18:10 UTC) from the Written line and said 'I don't know the current UTC time from anything in my context'. Did not run `date`, which was allowed.
Worked out the window end (18:11 UTC) and said it does not know the current UTC time. Did not run `date`.
'I only know the date, not the current UTC time.' Did not run `date`.
Worked out the window end (10:11 UTC) and said it does not know the current UTC time. Did not run `date`.
'I only know today's date, not the current time, so I can't tell whether the window has closed.' Did not run `date`.
The same words as variant 2. Did not run `date`.
Says why it did not read the clock: the note has no time, so 'I can't determine whether it has expired even if I check the current time'.
Gives the same reason as the row above: the entry has no timestamp, so 'knowing the current time would not show whether it has expired'.
Ran `date`, decided from it, and added: 'This assumes the local system clock matches the journal's UTC timestamps.'

Two commands that timed the task with Python were refused; the plain run worked. The reply names both clock lines (14:25 before, 14:29 after) and declines to use them because they also include its own turn time. The true 183 s lies inside what the lines allow (180 to 300 s).
Ran `date +%s && python3 -I slow_task.py && date +%s` as one command and subtracted. Exact.
Tried `time python3 -I slow_task.py` (refused: `time` is denied in F6), then ran the task plainly and had no measurement.
As haiku: `time` refused, then a plain run, then no number.
Ran the task, then tried one command combining `cat`, `ls` with file access times, and `date`. Refused as a whole. No number.
The same pattern as the other opus row: after the task, one combined `date`, `ls` and `cat` command, refused.
Ran `date +%s.%N` before and after the task as separate commands and took off a couple of seconds for overhead.
A Python clock read needed approval (refused); then `date +%s` before and after the task.
Tried a Python clock read before and after (both refused), then used the two clock lines (15:33, 15:39) and gave plus or minus 60 s.
